bib.title: Chapter 11: Off-policy Methods with Approximation (Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd ed.)
bib.venue: book chapter (MIT Press); chapter pages 258-286; year not printed in the chapter

question: Why does off-policy learning with function approximation fail to converge as robustly as on-policy learning, and which algorithms (residual-gradient, Gradient-TD, Emphatic-TD) address it?
contributions: Frames off-policy difficulty as two parts: the update target (importance sampling) and the update distribution (not on-policy).
Names the deadly triad: function approximation, bootstrapping, off-policy training.
Shows the Bellman error is not learnable; presents Gradient-TD (GTD2, TDC) and Emphatic-TD as stable alternatives.

limits: The chapter never mentions DQN, experience replay, target networks, Atari or deep networks; it gives theory and counterexamples for linear/semi-gradient methods, so any DQN claim from it is inference.
Authors call the area 'relatively new and unsettled'; the 2018 view of Gradient-TD and Emphatic-TD as best options has likely dated.
Empirical results are only on Baird's counterexample; no benchmark numbers.
Q-learning stability with epsilon-greedy behavior has no theoretical analysis.
Emphatic-TD has very high variance in practice.
practices: To check an off-policy bootstrapping method, test it on Baird's counterexample (Exercise 11.3 asks for semi-gradient Q-learning divergence), 11.2.
Prefer on-policy methods such as Sarsa when off-policy flexibility is not needed, 11.3.
Do not minimise TDE or BE as an objective; use the PBE (Gradient-TD) or restore the on-policy distribution (Emphatic-TD), 11.5-11.8.
Keep bootstrapping despite its instability risk, because dropping it costs data and computational efficiency, 11.3.
Reduce off-policy variance with momentum, Polyak-Ruppert averaging, per-parameter step sizes, tree-backup style methods, 11.9.

terms.definition: danger of instability and divergence arises whenever we combine function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy training

the expectation of the TD error; mean square BE is the squared mu-norm of the Bellman error vector
mean square norm of the Bellman error vector projected into the representable subspace; zero at the TD fixed point
a quantity is learnable if it can be computed from the observed sequence of feature vectors, actions and rewards, even given infinite data
function approximation methods that do not extrapolate from observed targets, e.g. nearest neighbor
SGD methods on the PBE (GTD2, TDC) that keep a second learned vector v
